Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. The billionaire tax measure, funded by one healthcare union, would put 90% of the money it collects toward the state’s healthcare program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal (https://calmatters.org/tag/medi-cal/). Newsom, along with many other leading California Democrats and most Republicans, has vocally opposed the billionaire tax and tried to negotiate to keep it off the ballot. In general during his two terms as governor he has opposed state-level taxes on assets, out of concern the wealthy will leave the state and deprive the state of their income tax revenue. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive
State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax
the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these
kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor
Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to
the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal
property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for
simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under
Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would
not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the
Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that
happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the
options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state
to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues
would be reduced is unclear.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership
of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish
new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.

# Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings
Proposition 42 is described as an effort to protect retirement and personal savings, but it’s also among two measures that could block a proposed billionaire tax intended to primarily fund healthcare.
...
### What will the measure do?
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
...
### Who are the supporters?
The California Small Business Assn., California Senior Alliance, California Professional Firefighters and other groups back the measure.
“Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California — we need protection against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings,” supporters wrote in favor of the measure.

## Proposition 42
**The basics**
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes.
But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound.
And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
...
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other.

PROPOSITION 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive
State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax
the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these
kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor
Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to
the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal
property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for
simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under
Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would
not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the
Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that
happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive
State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax
the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these
kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor
Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to
the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal
property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for
simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under
Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would
not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the
Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that
happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the
options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state
to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues
would be reduced is unclear.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership
of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish
new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. The billionaire tax could be defeated by two other tax measures. Here’s how

By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. 

The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it.

Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40, but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. 

“I don’t think that people at this point realize they're direct countermeasures because there hasn't been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC.

Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect.

What each measure does

Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. 

Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. 

Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit.

Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost.

Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Recent polling shows voters narrowly support Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax — and two measures designed to kill it. Only one outcome can prevail. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. Newsom argues the tax would not create a long-term solution to California’s budget woes and will drive wealthy people and businesses the state relies on through income taxes out of the state, further reducing revenue. Sergey Brin, the Google co-founder, and other billionaires are bankrolling the opposition campaign, ploughing more than $56 million into the No on Prop. 40 committee through a political organization called Building a Better California. That same group is the primary financial backer for both Propositions 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) and 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/), raising $131 million to campaign for those measures. In total, the billionaire-backed group has gathered more than $187 million to try to defeat Prop. 40. Baldassare said the billionaire tax’s backers will have a difficult time overcoming voter confusion about the three competing measures. The billionaire tax could be defeated by two other tax measures. Here’s how

By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. 

The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it.

Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40, but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. 

“I don’t think that people at this point realize they're direct countermeasures because there hasn't been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC.

Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect.

What each measure does

Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. 

Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. 

Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit.

Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost.

Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

If you oppose it, voting No on Prop 40 defeats it directly without the broader constitutional restrictions in 42, which would only act as a backup. If you support it, a No on 42 keeps it from being nullified, though a Yes on 40 with more votes than 42 would still take effect.

I'm working out whether a yes or no on Prop 42 can be answered without weighing in on the billionaire tax and constitutional lock-in, which are value questions. The SF Chronicle's point is that you can oppose the billionaire tax and still see 42's collateral damage as a reason to vote no.

The editorial boards are split on this one, with the Daily News backing yes as a limit on unreasonable tax increases and the LAO's revenue outlook unclear. Since the choice turns on how someone weighs the billionaire tax and constitutional lock-in, I'm not going to reduce it to one word.

I'm deciding not to give a bare yes or no, since whether 42 is the right call depends on how someone weighs the billionaire tax against a permanent constitutional limit on future taxes. I can still lay out the practical rule: a yes on 42 is the vote that could cancel Prop 40, while a no leaves 40 able to take effect if it gets more votes than 42.

Checking whether Prop 40 really exempts retirement accounts, pensions, and real estate, since the LAO says it generally does. Then I want to see whether there are actual proposals to tax retirement accounts or whether that's just a talking point, and I'll try to find CalMatters' explainer on Prop 42 to see how it frames that.

I'm going to check the CalMatters piece on how the billionaire tax could be defeated by the other tax measures, to see how far Prop 42 reaches. I also want to confirm who is funding each side, since Building a Better California is backing 42 and SEIU-UHW is opposing it.

Checking the campaign backers now: Building a Better California and the Chamber of Commerce and firefighter and trades groups on one side, with the Chronicle, the Bee, and Sanders and Khanna opposing. I still need to confirm where the state Democratic Party stands and whether the LAO's conflict warning means 42 would definitely override Prop 40.

I'm pulling up the CalMatters piece on how Prop 40 and 42 interact, and checking the Berkeley IGS endorsement table for Prop 42. I also want to find the California Democratic Party's stance on it.

content.text: The LAO's analysis is neutral: it says the revenue effect is possible but unclear. Two more checks: how the CalMatters explainer describes the two "poison pill" measures, and the newspaper endorsement table.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.

The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”

content.text:
I'm not going to give a one-word answer on this one. Whether Prop 42 is the better choice depends on values: whether you want the 5% billionaire tax (Prop 40) to take effect, and whether you want a permanent constitutional ban on new taxes on financial assets. I read the measure text, the LAO analysis, recent polls, and endorsements from both sides. Here's what matters so you can decide quickly.

**A yes vote**
- Bars new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, pensions, stocks, business interests, intellectual property, and other personal property, for taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026. Existing taxes and real estate are excluded.
- Bars retroactive taxes, with narrow emergency exceptions.
- Is written to void Prop 40 if Prop 42 gets more yes votes than Prop 40. The LAO notes that courts would have to decide whether the two conflict.
- Changing it would take another statewide vote.

**A no vote**
- Leaves the state free to create these taxes later, through the normal legislative or voter process.
- Doesn't void Prop 40. Prop 40 takes effect if it gets more yes votes than Props 41 and 42.

**Disputed points**
- Prop 40 generally excludes real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts (LAO). CalMatters reports there is no current proposal to tax 401(k)s. Yes backers cite six recent proposals and past asset-tax bills that stalled.
- The LAO says Prop 42 could reduce future tax revenue, by an amount it calls unclear.
- Support is close and slipping. PPIC (Oct. 16–22) had it at 51% yes, 47% no. Berkeley IGS/LA Times (late October) had it at 43% yes, 45% no. Prop 40 trails in both polls, so if it fails on its own, Prop 42's remaining effect is the permanent ban.
- Backers say the measure isn't aimed at Prop 40. Critics call it a poison pill.

**Coalitions**
- Yes: Gov. Newsom, California Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, CalChamber, and police and veterans' groups. About $128M in reported contributions through Oct. 22, mostly via Building a Better California, which Sergey Brin and other tech billionaires fund.
- No: California Democratic Party, SEIU-UHW (the union behind Prop 40), Bernie Sanders, and the SF Chronicle and Sacramento Bee editorial boards. About $23M in reported contributions.

**How to decide**
- If you want the billionaire tax to take effect, a yes on 42 (or 41) could void it.
- If you oppose the billionaire tax, a no on 40 is the direct way to stop it. Prop 42 matters only if 40 still wins a majority, and a yes on 42 also adds the permanent ban.
- If you're weighing the ban alone: do you want a permanent constitutional limit on future taxes on financial assets?

If you tell me which of these matters most to you, I can help you work through it.
